Room Design

►
Ground Floor Plane
Secondary Floor Plane
A second floor plane at its own height — for modelling a mezzanine, upper level, or raised platform above the ground floor.
Lower this to see through the secondary floor plane to whatever's above or below it — useful when checking a mezzanine or upper level against the ground floor.
Uncheck to give the secondary floor its own length/width/position/rotation instead of always mirroring the ground floor below.
Stairwell
Which way the stairwell opening faces: +Z/-Z run along the room's length, +X/-X run along its width.

Studio Walls

►
Tints each wall a different colour so you can tell them apart in the 3D view — purely visual, doesn't affect the walls themselves.
Rendering only — lightens or darkens the wall material in the 3D view, doesn't reflect a real paint or acoustic treatment value.
Drape Rail
Hangs from the truss (full height, truss to floor) along whichever sides you enable. Choose sides individually to leave a gap for an entrance.
0 = flat panel. Higher values fold the drape like real curtain pleats (folds per metre of width).

Primary Camera Ring

►
Global Settings
Horizontal and vertical field of view — how wide a cone each camera sees. Matched to the selected camera model by default; adjust here to model a different lens.
Effective capture distance — coverage calculations treat anything beyond this as unseen, even if it's within the FOV cone.
Draws the mounting truss around the room at camera height — visual/quoting aid only, doesn't affect coverage.
Sets the profile drawn for the ring truss, grid rails and legs, and the piece lengths in the Truss Component Report. F14, F24 and F34 are Global Truss 4-point box trusses, 100, 220 and 290 mm external. The same choice is in the Truss Designer's GAUGE dropdown. Visual and reporting aid only.
Adds vertical support legs to the truss report and 3D view — only relevant if truss is shown above.
Ground Floor Camera Counts
Also cycles with hotkey 7 in the 3D view, or by clicking a camera directly.

Secondary Camera Ring

►
A second, independent set of cameras — e.g. for a mezzanine level or a different height tier — on top of the Primary Camera Ring, not instead of it.
Global Settings
Secondary Floor Camera Counts

Camera positions follow the Secondary Floor Plane dimensions set in Room Design.

Individual & Grid Cameras

►

Individual Cameras

Automatically re-angles individual cameras to reduce coverage gaps and overlap, based on their current positions and FOV.

Camera Grid

Fills the room with an evenly-spaced top-down array — parametric like the Primary/Secondary Ring, so it updates live as you drag any control below or resize the room, rather than a one-off generator. Height here is independent of the camera rings' own height sliders. Because it fully regenerates on every change, it isn't meant for one-off per-camera hand-tweaking — use Individual Cameras above for that instead.
Type how many cameras you want and the grid works out the rows and columns that space them most evenly across the room (the Rows and Columns sliders then just show the result). If the number doesn't divide into a neat rectangle, some rows get one extra camera so the spacing stays even.
24 cameras, evenly spaced across the room.
Defaults to Slim Style so it reads differently from the Primary/Secondary Ring at a glance — independent of the camera model chosen above, since the visual style and the actual spec don't have to match.

Grid Truss

Simple beams positioned above the grid's camera height (matching how the Primary Ring's truss sits above its own cameras), aligned exactly with the grid's row and/or column positions and reaching to the room's edges — only drawn while the grid is enabled. Independent of the Primary/Secondary Ring's own truss. Defaults to a half-size lattice, since a dense grid with many rails can look cluttered at full truss scale — drop to Simple rail for the lightest look, or up to Full truss to match the rings exactly.
Draws the installation measurements for the grid truss rails: the spacing between adjacent rails, a margin dimension showing how far the first/last rail sits in from the wall whenever Rail margin is non-zero, the vertical gap from the rails up to the room's ceiling height, and — when Show truss is also enabled for the Primary Ring — a second vertical gap from the rails to that perimeter truss, since the two structures can sit at different heights and don't share a single drop figure. Requires Grid truss rails set to something other than Off. These are drawn directly into the 3D scene, so they appear in any screenshot you take once switched on.

Tripod Layout Designer

►
Enter the volume you need (e.g. 12 × 12 × 4 m) and the cameras you have; the planner finds the fewest cameras for 3+ camera coverage and can apply the layout.
For offsite shoots: stands in a ring outside the capture area (the Room Design floor), cameras clamped up each mast, cables across the floor and up each stand. Switching this on turns the Primary Ring cameras and truss off; switching it off puts them back.
Cameras are spread evenly from the top height down to the lowest.
Drag a stand in the 3D view to move it; its cameras and cables follow when you let go. Auto Optimise re-aims the stand cameras along with everything else.

Network Switches

►
Place switches up in the truss (or anywhere) to keep camera-to-switch Cat6A runs short — cameras auto-assign to their nearest switch when routing cables, with a manual override available per camera. One switch can be marked Bridge to aggregate the others and uplink to the equipment rack.
Star: every edge switch uplinks directly to the Bridge switch. Daisy-chain: each switch uplinks to whichever neighbouring switch is nearest and closer to the rack, hopping switch to switch until reaching the Bridge (or the rack, if there's no Bridge). Either way, the Bridge's own uplink always goes straight to the equipment rack. Requires at least one rack in the scene and Cables enabled to draw these — shown as thicker lines, colour-matched to the switch they originate from.

Volumetric System

►
4DViews HOLOSYS pod ring — centres in your current room and checks it fits (min. 9m x 9m floor + 4m ceiling, per 4DViews). Includes each pod's real 4-camera arrangement, incl. overhead cameras on every 2nd pod. Heights above the confirmed 0.10m floor cameras are estimates — verify against your rig.
When enabled, these ring/leg components are automatically included in the Truss Component Report alongside any rectangular truss.
0 = flat panel. Higher values fold the drape like real curtain pleats (folds per metre of width).
Truss height is a placement aid, not vendor spec — stay under your ceiling height minus safe clearance above the ~3m overhead cameras.
Positioned just outside the camera ring so they can't block any camera's view — visual on/off only, not an actual scene light source.
Chroma-key green disc matching the drape/truss ring radius — independent of the drape's own colour choice above.

Visualisation

►
Opacity of the camera field-of-view wireframe cones — lower to see through overlapping coverage, raise for a clearer read of individual camera angles.
Opacity of the truss/pipework rendering — lower it if the truss is visually cluttering the view of cameras and coverage underneath.
The 2D coverage map shows which floor cells are seen by how many cameras at THIS height off the ground — e.g. set to ~1.7m to check coverage at head height rather than at the floor.
Draws each camera's field-of-view as a cone/pyramid, so you can see exactly what it can and can't see.
Cuts the FOV wireframes off at floor level instead of letting them pass through it — usually clearer for checking floor-level coverage.
Colours the actual 3D capture volume by how many cameras see each point — red/orange/green/bright-green for 1/2/3/4+ cameras.
Same colour-by-camera-count idea, but as a flat floor-level heatmap at the Coverage height set above — quicker to read at a glance than the full 3D view.

Brain Bar

The rack of processing/recording equipment operators work from during a shoot — shown here mainly for spatial planning (cable runs, sightlines to the volume).
An average-height human figure, purely for gauging scale in the 3D view — not a real capture subject or a camera target.

If the app's virtual North doesn't match real/magnetic North on site, set the angle between them here — every camera bearing shown in the Alignment tool adjusts to match, so it reads correctly against a compass in the room.
Lower to see through the ground floor, e.g. to check a secondary floor plane or basement level underneath.

Import Floorplan

►
Import a floor plan image to display under the studio floor. Scale it to match your room dimensions, then use Ground plane opacity below to make the studio floor transparent so you can see through to the image.
Keeps the image's own proportions when you change Width or Height below, so it doesn't stretch or squash — uncheck to size width/height independently.

►

SELECTED OBJECT
All three combine — if the model came in lying on its side or facing the wrong way, tilt/roll first to stand it upright, then use Turn to face the direction you want.

1.0×

Import Point Cloud

►
Bring in a site scan (laser scan or Gaussian Splat capture, exported as binary .ply) as a visual reference for planning against real mounting points — walls, an existing ceiling grid, obstructions. This is a reference layer, not part of the design itself: it's excluded from client-facing exports, and doesn't persist in Save Layout (re-import after loading a saved layout).
Most laser scan and survey software treats Z as vertical; this app treats Y as vertical. If the cloud looks like it's lying on its side or standing on end, toggle this.
Position/rotation here just nudge the cloud to line up with the room. Scans are often, but not always, at true real-world scale — if it looks off, use Scale Calibration below rather than guessing at a scale slider.
SCALE CALIBRATION
Laser scans and Gaussian Splat captures are usually genuinely accurate at real-world scale — if the room looks off, it's more often the room dimensions that need correcting to match the scan, not the other way round. Click two points on the cloud with a known real distance between them (a doorway width, the ceiling grid spacing), then scale whichever one is actually wrong.
Click a point on the cloud…
Replaces the scan's own colours — useful if they're washed out, or for a cleaner look in a client-facing capture.

Quick Start Tutorial
About 5 minutes

New to TARGET3D? This walks through building a first camera layout end to end. If you'd rather have it shown to you directly in the app, use the button below.

  1. Pick a starting point. Open the Presets section and click one of the 8 built-in system presets — the scene builds itself instantly. Or start from scratch if your layout is unusual.
  2. Set your room size. Use the Room Design sliders for length and width. Double-click any blue value in the panel to type an exact number.
  3. Place your cameras. Under Camera Count, set how many cameras go on each wall, pick a camera model, and set height and field of view.
  4. Check your coverage. Turn on 2D or 3D coverage under Visualise, or run Auto Optimise for a one-click pass that aims every camera for maximum coverage.
  5. Save your work. Use Save Current as Preset, or Share Design to generate a link that encodes the whole session — no account needed.

Next: Optimising Coverage covers the aiming tools in more depth.

Tutorial de Inicio Rápido
Unos 5 minutos

¿Nuevo en TARGET3D? Esta guía recorre la construcción de una primera disposición de cámaras de principio a fin. Si prefieres verlo directamente en la aplicación, usa el botón de abajo.

  1. Elige un punto de partida. Abre la sección Preajustes y haz clic en uno de los 8 preajustes de sistema incluidos — la escena se construye al instante. O empieza desde cero si tu disposición es poco habitual.
  2. Define el tamaño de la sala. Usa los deslizadores de Diseño de Sala para el largo y el ancho. Haz doble clic en cualquier valor azul del panel para escribir un número exacto.
  3. Coloca tus cámaras. En Recuento de Cámaras, define cuántas cámaras hay en cada pared, elige un modelo de cámara y ajusta la altura y el campo de visión.
  4. Comprueba la cobertura. Activa la cobertura 2D o 3D en Visualizar, o ejecuta Auto Optimizar para un ajuste automático que apunta todas las cámaras hacia la máxima cobertura.
  5. Guarda tu trabajo. Usa Guardar Actual como Preajuste, o Compartir Diseño para generar un enlace que codifica toda la sesión — sin necesidad de cuenta.

Siguiente: Optimizar la Cobertura profundiza en las herramientas de puntería.

Performance Capture Setup
About 8 minutes

A walkthrough for dual-height rigs — typically a high ring for full-body tracking and a low ring for detail, sometimes across two physical floor levels.

  1. Start from a baseline. The Performance Capture preset in Presets gives you a sensible dual-ring starting point, or build manually from an empty room.
  2. Enable the Secondary Camera Ring. Set its height and per-wall camera counts independently of the primary ring.
  3. Decide if you have a real second floor. Only tick Show floor plane under Secondary Floor Plane if there's an actual raised floor or mezzanine at that height. If your second ring is just a lower set of cameras on the same floor, leave it unticked — the secondary ring's cameras will then contribute to primary floor coverage rather than being optimised as a separate zone. See Cameras for the full explanation.
  4. Run Auto Optimise. With the floor plane off, every camera optimises together for one continuous floor. With it on, the ground and secondary zones optimise independently.
  5. Fine-tune if needed. Use the Floor Select or Volume Select Tool to aim cameras at a specific capture area or height range by hand.

See also: Multi-Floor Layouts for mezzanines and staircases.

Configuración de Performance Capture
Unos 8 minutos

Una guía para montajes de doble altura — normalmente un anillo alto para el seguimiento de cuerpo completo y un anillo bajo para el detalle, a veces repartidos en dos niveles de suelo físicos.

  1. Parte de una base. El preajuste Performance Capture en Preajustes te da un punto de partida razonable con doble anillo, o constrúyelo manualmente desde una sala vacía.
  2. Activa el Anillo de Cámaras Secundario. Ajusta su altura y el número de cámaras por pared de forma independiente del anillo primario.
  3. Decide si tienes un segundo suelo real. Marca Mostrar plano de suelo en Plano de Suelo Secundario solo si hay un suelo elevado o entreplanta real a esa altura. Si tu segundo anillo es solo un conjunto de cámaras más bajas en el mismo suelo, déjalo sin marcar — así las cámaras del anillo secundario contribuirán a la cobertura del suelo primario en lugar de optimizarse como zona aparte. Consulta Cámaras para la explicación completa.
  4. Ejecuta Auto Optimizar. Con el plano de suelo desactivado, todas las cámaras se optimizan juntas para un único suelo continuo. Con él activado, las zonas de suelo y secundaria se optimizan de forma independiente.
  5. Ajusta manualmente si lo necesitas. Usa la Herramienta de Selección de Suelo o de Volumen para apuntar cámaras a un área o rango de altura de captura específico a mano.

Ver también: Diseños Multi-Planta para entreplantas y escaleras.

Building a Custom Truss
About 10 minutes

For layouts the auto-generated truss doesn't quite match — asymmetric rooms, specific ground supports, or a layout with obstructions to route around.

  1. Open the designer. Visualise menu → Manual Truss Designer.
  2. Bring in a starting point. Click Import Auto Truss to copy the current auto-generated layout in as an editable one, or start from an empty grid.
  3. Choose which ring you're editing. The Ring toggle switches between the Primary and Secondary truss — each keeps its own independent layout.
  4. Draw your layout. Use Run to draw truss segments between nodes, Leg to drop a straight support to the floor, and Erase to remove a segment (or wipe-shorten an open end by dragging inward).
  5. Go 3D if you need to. Turn on Freeform to place points at custom heights, connect nodes between the Primary and Secondary layers, or connect down to a floor anchor point for a custom-angled ground support.
  6. Bake it in. Click Apply to Model when you're happy, or Clear / Revert to Auto to start over.

Full reference: Truss & Structure.

Construir una Estructura Personalizada
Unos 10 minutos

Para disposiciones que la estructura generada automáticamente no cubre del todo bien — salas asimétricas, apoyos a suelo específicos, o un diseño con obstáculos que hay que rodear.

  1. Abre el diseñador. Menú Visualizar → Diseñador de Estructura Manual.
  2. Parte de una base. Haz clic en Importar Estructura Automática para copiar el diseño autogenerado actual como uno editable, o empieza desde una cuadrícula vacía.
  3. Elige qué anillo estás editando. El interruptor de Anillo cambia entre la estructura Primaria y Secundaria — cada una mantiene su propio diseño independiente.
  4. Dibuja tu diseño. Usa Tramo para dibujar segmentos de estructura entre nodos, Pata para bajar un apoyo recto hasta el suelo, y Borrar para eliminar un segmento (o acortar un extremo abierto arrastrando hacia dentro).
  5. Pasa a 3D si lo necesitas. Activa Forma Libre para colocar puntos a alturas personalizadas, conectar nodos entre las capas Primaria y Secundaria, o conectar hacia abajo con un punto de anclaje en el suelo para un apoyo a suelo con ángulo personalizado.
  6. Consolídalo. Haz clic en Aplicar al Modelo cuando estés conforme, o Borrar Todo / Volver a Automático para empezar de nuevo.

Referencia completa: Estructura y Truss.

Optimising Coverage
About 6 minutes

Getting the most out of your camera placement — automatically, or aimed precisely where you need it.

  1. Visualise what cameras can see. Turn on 2D or 3D coverage under Visualise to see the current coverage as a heatmap or volume.
  2. Let the tool do it. Run Auto Optimise for a one-click pass that maximises floor and volume coverage across all cameras.
  3. Target a specific area. Use the Floor Select Tool: paint the cells that matter, then click Aim to Selection.
  4. Target a specific height range. Use the Volume Select Tool the same way, with a height range set in its HUD — useful for a stage, riser, or raised platform.
  5. Keep the view clean. Use Hide Selection to tuck the highlighted tiles out of the way without losing your selection or the resulting camera aim.

Full reference: Coverage & Visualisation.

Optimizar la Cobertura
Unos 6 minutos

Saca el máximo partido a la colocación de tus cámaras — automáticamente, o apuntando con precisión donde lo necesites.

  1. Visualiza lo que ven las cámaras. Activa la cobertura 2D o 3D en Visualizar para ver la cobertura actual como mapa de calor o volumen.
  2. Deja que la herramienta lo haga. Ejecuta Auto Optimizar para un ajuste de un solo clic que maximiza la cobertura de suelo y volumen en todas las cámaras.
  3. Apunta a un área concreta. Usa la Herramienta de Selección de Suelo: pinta las celdas que importan y haz clic en Apuntar a la Selección.
  4. Apunta a un rango de altura concreto. Usa la Herramienta de Selección de Volumen de la misma forma, con un rango de altura definido en su panel — útil para un escenario, tarima o plataforma elevada.
  5. Mantén la vista despejada. Usa Ocultar Selección para retirar las celdas resaltadas sin perder tu selección ni el encuadre de cámara resultante.

Referencia completa: Cobertura y Visualización.

Sharing & Quoting
About 5 minutes

Turning a finished layout into something you can send to a client.

  1. Save or share your layout. Save it as a named preset for later, or use Share Design to generate a link that encodes the whole session — no account or upload needed, works offline.
  2. Switch to Quote Builder. Line items are pulled automatically from what's actually in your 3D scene.
  3. Adjust as needed. Change quantities or pricing, or add extra line items by hand.
  4. Preview the proposal. Switch to the Proposal tab for a client-ready layout, then print or export it.
  5. Push it to Pipedrive. Click Send to Pipedrive in the top bar, search for the deal, and post a design summary, quote summary, or a screengrab of the 3D view straight onto it. Requires a one-time setup by whoever manages the site deployment — see PIPEDRIVE_SETUP.md.
  6. Add the kit list to the deal as products. In Send to Pipedrive, choose the deal, then Add kit list to deal as products. Each line of the open quote is matched to a Pipedrive product by its SKU (the product's code) and you get a review list before anything is sent:
    • Prices are Pipedrive's catalogue price in the deal's currency. Any price can be changed in the review; lines whose Pipedrive price is 0 or missing are flagged. Many catalogue products only have a EUR price, so for a GBP deal you can tick Where Pipedrive has no GBP price, use the quote's price (off by default)
    • No match? The line goes in as Pipedrive's Custom product, with its description and SKU in the comment and the quote's price. Or pick a product from the list, or Search Pipedrive… by name or code, or skip the line
    • VAT comes from each quote line; the quote's discount can be applied to every line (tick box)
    • Products already on the deal are kept; the kit list is added after them. Adding needs two taps, and warns if you add the same list twice
    • Products you choose for a SKU are remembered on this device, so next time those lines match straight away
    Then generate the quote from the deal with your Pipedrive quote template as usual.

Full reference: Save, Load & Export.

Compartir y Presupuestar
Unos 5 minutos

Convertir un diseño terminado en algo que puedas enviar a un cliente.

  1. Guarda o comparte tu diseño. Guárdalo como preajuste con nombre para más tarde, o usa Compartir Diseño para generar un enlace que codifica toda la sesión — sin cuenta ni subida de archivos, funciona sin conexión.
  2. Cambia al Generador de Presupuestos. Las líneas del presupuesto se extraen automáticamente de lo que hay realmente en tu escena 3D.
  3. Ajusta lo que haga falta. Cambia cantidades o precios, o añade líneas adicionales a mano.
  4. Previsualiza la propuesta. Cambia a la pestaña Propuesta para un diseño listo para el cliente, y luego imprímelo o expórtalo.
  5. Envíalo a Pipedrive. Haz clic en Enviar a Pipedrive en la barra superior, busca el trato, y publica un resumen del diseño, del presupuesto o una captura de la vista 3D directamente en él. Requiere una configuración inicial por parte de quien gestione el despliegue del sitio — consulta PIPEDRIVE_SETUP.md.

Referencia completa: Guardar, Cargar y Exportar.

Getting Started

Site visit

The Site visit tab (first tab, before System Designer) is the Target3D site visit form, v1.5.0, built in. It has two sub-tabs under its title: Site survey for a room before installation (a new visit starts here) and Health check for an existing installation. Visit details, Photos & notes, Topics covered and Export are shared by both. Switching sub-tab keeps both sets of entries, but the report notes, Pipedrive note and PDF only include the one you are on, and the visit purpose changes to match unless you typed your own. The form also has its own detailed Help at the bottom (tap its version number).

Visits in this design — the bar at the top of the tab:

  • A design can hold several visits, for example a pre-install survey followed by yearly health checks. Pick one from the list to open it; + New visit starts another, and Delete removes the one shown after asking. The form's own Start a new visit button also adds a visit rather than wiping the current one
  • Visits save in this browser as you type, and travel with the design in Save Layout / Load Layout and share links. Saved presets leave them out, since presets are design templates
  • ☾ Dark / ☀ Light, in the top bar next to EN/ES, switches the whole app between dark and light: every tab, menu and dialog. The quote card in Quote Builder and the proposal page stay white like paper in both themes (they are documents), printing and PDFs are unchanged, and the 3D view keeps its own background setting. Until you use it the app follows your device's setting; after that it remembers your choice on this device
  • A new visit takes its client from the design (Proposal or Quote client), and its Pipedrive deal from the deal chosen in Send to Pipedrive. Linking a deal in a visit also selects it in Send to Pipedrive if none is chosen there. Neither ever overwrites something you typed

Shared sections

  • Visit details — Who, where and when. Add a contact for each person you dealt with at the client, and anyone else present under Other attendees.
  • Pipedrive record — Choose Deal, Lead or Project, then type the deal number (for example 10599) or part of the name and tap Find. Tap the right result to link it; the record’s title is shown so you can check it. In System Designer, lookups use System Designer’s own Pipedrive connection, so there is nothing to connect. If Pipedrive can’t be reached, you can still enter a deal number: it is saved unchecked and appears in the report notes.
  • Photos & notes — Log each photo you take with a caption, in the order you take them, so the images can be matched to captions later. The photos themselves stay on your camera roll. Use Anything else for loose notes and reminders.
  • Topics covered — Your checklist for the conversation with the client. Tick each topic as you cover it; the counter shows how many are done. For Other, tick it and type what you talked about. Ticked topics go into the report notes, and anything unticked is listed as not covered so you can pick it up next time.

Health check sections

  • System — What is installed and the state it was in when you arrived. Record the software version on arrival and on departure, even if they are the same, so the report shows whether anything was updated.
  • Health check — Tap OK, Issue or N/A for each item and add a note when there is something worth recording. Tap the same button again to clear it. Items you leave untouched are listed as “not checked”. Use Add your own check for anything specific to the site.
  • Actions taken on site — Things you changed or did: updates, settings, repairs, tests. One action per entry.
  • Findings — Anything the client should know about, with a short explanation of why it matters. Set a severity so the report can sort critical items to the top.
  • Training — Tick the box if training was delivered, list who attended, and add a session for each block of the agenda with the topics covered, one per line.
  • Recommendations — Upgrades or changes you discussed. Priority (Recommended, Optional or Next step) controls how each one is shown in the report summary.
  • Follow-up — Demos, return visits, deadlines or anything promised to the client.

Site survey sections

  • Pre-survey — Preparation before you arrive. Mark each item Done, Issue or N/A, and write down the survey objectives so the report starts from what the client needs.
  • Room assessment — Measurements in metres, then the room checklist. Usable area is the clear space left once obstructions are taken off. Note anything that could affect optical tracking, such as windows, IR sources and reflective surfaces. Use in System Designer copies the room length, width and height into the design’s room size and wall height; it shows you what will change first.
  • Infrastructure — Power and network as you find them, whether more is needed, and how cables could be routed.
  • Access & logistics — How equipment gets in. The maximum equipment size is the largest item that fits through the tightest point on the route.
  • Technical — Mounting options, equipment positions and integration needs, plus your technical recommendations for the design.
  • Challenges & risks — One entry per challenge, with its impact (Low, Medium or High) and how you would deal with it.
  • Site readiness — Your verdict on whether the room is suitable, what needs to change if not, and how many days the install should take.
  • Actions & next steps — Each action with an owner, a due date and a status (Open, In progress or Done).

Use in System Designer (Room assessment) copies the surveyed room into the design: length and width become the ground length and width, and the height becomes Wall height (Studio Walls), which is also the ceiling the Dims overlay measures to. It lists every change and asks first, warns if the camera height is above the new height, and widens a slider if the room is bigger than its range or measured to the centimetre. Usable area, ceiling type and maximum equipment size have no matching design setting, so they stay in the visit (and its report notes).

Export, Pipedrive and PDF

  • Export — Tap Copy report notes, paste them into a Claude chat and ask for the site visit report, attaching your photos in the same message. If you don’t have the report template in your own Claude chats, send the notes and photos to whoever writes the reports instead. Refresh preview shows what will be copied.
  • Send to Pipedrive — Adds the visit notes as a pinned note on the linked deal, lead or project. Tap once, then tap again to confirm. It sends whatever the form holds at that moment, so you can send again after more changes; each send adds a new note. If Pipedrive doesn’t confirm, check the record’s Notes before trying again.
  • Save PDF — Creates a Target3D-branded PDF of the visit notes and saves it to your device. Add PDF to Pipedrive attaches the same PDF to the linked deal or lead in one step; tap it twice to confirm. Projects can’t receive files this way, so for a project drag the PDF into its Files tab yourself. Photos are not included, only the photo log captions.
  • How Pipedrive is reached — through System Designer's own server functions on this site (the same connection as Send to Pipedrive; the API token never reaches the browser). Finding deals, leads and projects, pinned notes, and PDFs on deals and leads all work on the live site. On a copy without those functions (for example opened locally) the form says Pipedrive isn't reachable, but a deal number can still be saved unchecked

Backups — Copy backup in Export gives text starting T3D-SITE-VISIT-BACKUP, the same format as the standalone form, so a visit can move either way between the standalone form and System Designer with nothing lost. Paste it into Restore backup to bring a visit back into the visit shown.

The form is in English. It runs in its own frame inside the tab, so its phone and tablet layout and Target3D styling are exactly those of the standalone form.

Overview

TARGET3D System Designer lets you plan motion-capture studio layouts in 3D. Configure room dimensions, camera placements, truss structures, and more — then export a quote automatically.

  • Site visit tab — health check and site survey form, linked to Pipedrive and to this design
  • System Designer tab — interactive 3D viewport with controls panel
  • Quote Builder tab — add products and generate a pricing quote
  • Proposal tab — preview and print a client proposal
  • Help tab — this guide
  • ☾ Dark / ☀ Light and EN / ES in the top bar — light or dark for the whole app, and the interface language

Quick Start Presets

The fastest way to get started. Open the Presets section at the top of the left panel and click any of the 8 system presets — the scene rebuilds instantly, clearing all previous assets.

  • Virtual Production 12×8m · LED wall · 12× Prime X22 on full perimeter truss · brain bar · cables · 2D coverage at 1.5m
  • Perf Capture 10×10m · dual camera ring (40+ Prime X13 high & low) · brain bar at edge · 2D coverage at floor
  • LBVR 20×20m maze · 4 L-shaped partitions · 6 people · Slim X22 · 2D coverage at head height
  • Sports Science 8×5m · 10× Prime X41 · brain bar · person centred · 2D at floor
  • Outdoor Drone 20×10m · VersaX 41 at 8m height · 2D at floor
  • VR Lab 6×6m · 4× Vive Basestation corners · person centred · 2D at head height
  • Broadcast XR 10×8m · LED wall · 8× FLIR/Captury · brain bar opposite LED · cables
  • Multi-Floor 10×10m + 6×6m mezzanine · staircase · two 2D heat maps

You can save your own custom setups using Save Current as Preset at the bottom of the Presets panel.

Setting Room Dimensions

Use the Room Design sliders in the left controls panel. Tip: double-click any blue value in the panel to type an exact number to 2 decimal places — press Enter to confirm or Escape to cancel.

  • Room length (X) — depth of the studio in metres (up to 50m)
  • Room width (Z) — width of the studio in metres (up to 50m)
  • The 3D view updates in real-time as you drag sliders

Navigating the 3D View

  • Left-click drag — orbit / rotate the view
  • Right-click drag — pan the view
  • Scroll wheel — zoom in / out
  • Use the View menu → Viewport Angle buttons for Front, Side, Top, and 3D perspectives
  • Click Reset View to return to the default angle
Primeros Pasos

Resumen

TARGET3D System Designer te permite planificar diseños de estudios de captura de movimiento en 3D. Configura las dimensiones de la sala, la colocación de cámaras, las estructuras de truss y mucho más — y luego exporta un presupuesto automáticamente.

  • Pestaña Diseñador de Sistema — vista 3D interactiva con panel de controles
  • Pestaña Generador de Presupuestos — añade productos y genera un presupuesto
  • Pestaña Propuesta — previsualiza e imprime una propuesta para el cliente
  • Pestaña Ayuda — esta guía

Preajustes Quick Start

La forma más rápida de empezar. Abre la sección Preajustes en la parte superior del panel izquierdo y haz clic en cualquiera de los 8 preajustes de sistema — la escena se reconstruye al instante, eliminando todos los recursos anteriores.

  • Producción Virtual 12×8 m · pantalla LED · 12× Prime X22 en estructura perimetral completa · brain bar · cables · cobertura 2D a 1,5 m
  • Perf Capture 10×10 m · doble anillo de cámaras (40+ Prime X13 altas y bajas) · brain bar en el borde · cobertura 2D en el suelo
  • LBVR laberinto de 20×20 m · 4 particiones en L · 6 personas · Slim X22 · cobertura 2D a altura de cabeza
  • Ciencia del Deporte 8×5 m · 10× Prime X41 · brain bar · persona centrada · 2D en el suelo
  • Dron Exterior 20×10 m · VersaX 41 a 8 m de altura · 2D en el suelo
  • Laboratorio VR 6×6 m · 4× Vive Basestation en las esquinas · persona centrada · 2D a altura de cabeza
  • Difusión XR 10×8 m · pantalla LED · 8× FLIR/Captury · brain bar frente a la pantalla LED · cables
  • Multi-Planta 10×10 m + entreplanta de 6×6 m · escalera · dos mapas de calor 2D

Puedes guardar tus propias configuraciones personalizadas con Guardar Actual como Preajuste, al final del panel de Preajustes.

Ajustar las Dimensiones de la Sala

Usa los deslizadores de Diseño de Sala en el panel de controles izquierdo. Consejo: haz doble clic en cualquier valor azul del panel para escribir un número exacto con 2 decimales — pulsa Intro para confirmar o Escape para cancelar.

  • Largo de la sala (X) — profundidad del estudio en metros (hasta 50 m)
  • Ancho de la sala (Z) — anchura del estudio en metros (hasta 50 m)
  • La vista 3D se actualiza en tiempo real al mover los deslizadores

Navegar por la Vista 3D

  • Clic izquierdo y arrastrar — orbitar / rotar la vista
  • Clic derecho y arrastrar — desplazar la vista (pan)
  • Rueda del ratón — acercar / alejar (zoom)
  • Usa el menú Vista → botones de Ángulo de Vista para las perspectivas Frontal, Lateral, Superior y 3D
  • Haz clic en Restablecer Vista para volver al ángulo predeterminado

Changelog

Changelog (since v2.0)

v2.104.2 changes: Fixes from Josh's testing. Camera Alignment works on stand cameras: each stand's grab zone ran up the mast and caught clicks meant for its cameras (that also stopped aim arrows and style clicks on them); it is now round the base only, and a camera always wins over the stand it sits on. Also fixed: clicking an individual, grid or stand camera changed the Primary Ring's 3D style instead of its own. Layouts save more: the floorplan image and its size, position, rotation and opacity, truss drapes, Volumetric (HOLOSYS) options, north offset and floor opacity were never saved; they are now (large floorplans are shrunk to 2000 px). Presets and share links leave the floorplan image out. Load Layout opens .json files (button or drop) and accepts pasted text with stray bits round it; when something can't be loaded it says why in the box instead of a generic pop-up. Save Layout downloads a .json file. Imported 3D models and point clouds still need importing again. Checked in a real browser: every Visualise and Export item on a tripod design, Camera Alignment by mouse, and save → load of a design with a floorplan.

v2.104.1 changes: Tripod Stands is now the Tripod Layout Designer, and its cameras work with every aiming tool. Two gaps fixed: Floor Select / Volume Select → Aim to Selection skipped stand cameras when Show individual cameras was off, and Aim to Centre didn't reset stand cameras after a Volume Planner Apply. Stand cameras are no longer listed in the Individual Cameras list (edits there were lost when the stands regenerated); a line says how many there are. New Help card: what stand cameras work with and what doesn't apply. Checked in a real browser: FOV wireframes, 2D and 3D coverage, Auto Optimise, Aim to Centre and Aim to Selection all use the stand cameras.

v2.104.0 changes: Two additions requested by Josh. Tripod Stands rigging for offsite shoots on 3.2 m PA stands: stands in a ring outside the capture area (number, distance, cameras per stand, top and lowest heights, camera model), draggable stands, cables down each stand and across the floor, stand cameras included in coverage, Auto Optimise, reports and the quote (a Tripod PA stand line per stand). Switching it on turns the Primary Ring and truss off and back on again. Volume Planner (Plan a capture volume…): enter the volume (e.g. 12 × 12 × 4 m), rigging and the camera models you have; for each model it finds the fewest cameras so a marker anywhere in the volume, facing any way, is seen by 3+ cameras, and Apply sets the layout and aims. Also fixed: generated quotes never counted individual or grid cameras (the quote couldn't see them); they are counted now. Help: new Tripods & Volume Planner page, and what Auto Optimise does and doesn't cover.

v2.103.1 changes: Two fixes reported by Josh. Moving a person no longer hides the secondary camera ring. Dragging a person (and ticking or unticking Show person) rebuilt the cameras with an old copy of the camera code that only knew the primary ring and individual cameras, so the secondary ring vanished and Auto Optimise / global aims were reset to the room centre. Both now use the same camera builder as everything else, so the cameras and their aims stay exactly as they were. Typing a value, then using the slider, updates the value again. Double-clicking a blue value to type it replaced the label with a new copy, while the slider kept updating the original, so the shown number stopped following the slider; the original label is now kept. This applied to every slider with a typed value, not only Room Design. Both checked in a real browser against v2.103.0, which showed each bug.

v2.103.0 changes: Kit list to Pipedrive deal products. New button in Send to Pipedrive, Add kit list to deal as products: matches each line of the open quote to a Pipedrive product by SKU/product code, shows a review list (Pipedrive catalogue prices in the deal's currency, editable; flags for £0 or missing prices, with an optional tick box to use the quote's price where Pipedrive has none in that currency; pick, search or skip any line), then adds them to the deal in one go so the deal's own quote template can be used. Lines with no match go in as the Pipedrive product "Custom" with the description and SKU in the comment and the quote's price. VAT comes from the quote lines and the quote discount can be applied. Existing deal products are kept. Choices are remembered per SKU on this device. New server function pipedrive-deal-products (the API token stays on the server).

v2.102.0 changes: Light/Dark now themes the whole app. Light turns System Designer, Help, the top bar, menus and dialogs light; Dark turns Quote Builder, Proposal and the slide-out Quote panel dark. The quote card and proposal page stay white like paper, printing and PDFs are unchanged, and the 3D view keeps its own background setting. Each theme's original look is untouched (checked pixel for pixel). How: a small theme engine reads the app's own colours and derives the other theme, copying colour rules with the same specificity so the layout and states (hover, active, disabled) behave as before, and recolouring inline styles as scripts write them.

v2.101.0 changes: Light/Dark is now a global toggle in the top bar, next to EN/ES, instead of a button in the Site visit tab. It is one app-wide setting: until used the app follows the device, then it remembers the choice on this device (a choice already made in the Site visit tab carries over). Today it switches the Site visit form, the part of the app with both themes; the rest of the interface is unchanged, and the 3D view keeps its own separate background setting. The setting is also exposed on the page (data-ui-theme) so other parts can follow it as they gain light themes. Checked in a real browser: the toggle works from any tab, the form follows it, and the choice survives opening a new tab.

v2.100.0 changes: Site visit tab: Site survey first, and a Light/Dark button. In the form (now v1.6.0) Site survey is the first sub-tab, before Health check, a new visit starts as a site survey, and its Help lists the survey sections first; visits and backups that are already health checks stay health checks, and backups and report notes are unchanged. New ☾ Dark / ☀ Light button in the visits bar: the form follows the device until it is used, then remembers the choice on this device (it applies the form's own Target3D dark and light themes, with no white flash on loading). On narrow phones the bar's buttons shorten to "+ New", "Delete" and the icon so the visit list keeps its room. Checked in a real browser at 320 px and desktop, in both themes.

v2.99.1 changes: Fix: duplicate headers in the Site visit tab. The form's in-page links (the section buttons along its top, How to, the version number and Go to section in its Help) are #section links; inside the tab's frame the browser resolved them against System Designer's own address, so tapping one loaded a second copy of System Designer inside the form. The form (now v1.5.1) handles those links itself and scrolls to the section, landing exactly where the standalone form does; and if the frame is ever sent elsewhere, System Designer puts the form back automatically. Patch release: from here on versions use full Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH). Checked in a real browser by clicking each kind of link and by forcing the frame to navigate away.

v2.99 changes: New Site visit tab, before System Designer: the Target3D site visit form (health check and site survey) built in, as form v1.5.0. It runs in its own frame so its tested phone and tablet layout is unchanged, and its data model, backups and report notes are identical to the standalone v1.4.0 form, so visits move either way. Pipedrive goes through this site's server functions: a new pipedrive-find function finds a deal by number or searches deals, leads and projects; pipedrive-add-note now also takes leads and projects, HTML notes and pinning; pipedrive-add-file now also takes leads (projects are refused rather than risk an unlinked file). Existing Send to Pipedrive summaries behave exactly as before. New Add PDF to Pipedrive in the form's Export. Several visits per design, saved with Save Layout and share links (not presets); new visits take the client from the design and the deal from Send to Pipedrive. Use in System Designer in Room assessment copies the surveyed length, width and height into the design after asking. Also: loading a layout no longer rounds a saved value to a slider's step or caps it at the slider's range (a 16.25 m room or 7 m wall came back as 16.3 m / 6 m); the floating Quote tab hides on the Site visit tab; the Save Quote and Print buttons now really are hidden outside Quote Builder, as the code always intended; and on phones the top bar scrolls sideways within itself so every tab is reachable. Tested in a real browser at 320 px, phone landscape and tablet sizes, plus 41 end-to-end checks against a simulated Pipedrive (find, link, pinned notes, PDFs, Use in System Designer, several visits, save and load, a v1.4.0 backup restoring with every field intact, and report notes matching the standalone form line for line).

v2.98 changes: Copyright to Ashley Keeler and copy protection. Copyright notices added in the page source header, page metadata, under the app title, in a new Copyright & Licence Help card (English and Spanish), in the browser console, and in every saved layout file (generator and copyright fields). Hidden ownership markers that survive minifying: the notice is a plain string in the code, and the app title carries an invisible fingerprint. Edition-aware domain lock: this full edition (prices, Pipedrive) only runs on keeler.netlify.app and its Netlify previews (plus localhost for testing); a public edition flag allows ashleykeeler.com instead, so the full edition refuses to run on the public site. Anywhere else — including a saved copy opened from disk — shows a copyright notice with links to ashleykeeler.com instead of the tool. This is a deterrent rather than real security. Verified by the regression suite (new section 9): notices present, and the host check allows and blocks the right addresses for both editions.

v2.97 changes: Person figure: hands now on the ends of the arms, and a height marker. The hands had fixed positions that didn't match the tilted arms — each sat about 3 cm up the arm and 3.5 cm off to the side, so they looked detached. They are now worked out from the arm's own length, tilt and position, centred on the arm's line just past its tip. New View → Person Height toggle (on by default) shows a yellow measuring line from the floor to the top of each person's head with a 1.75 m label, taken from the figure's actual geometry. The markers live in their own group rather than in the people group, because the people group is copied whole into client GLB exports and every mesh in it blocks camera views; the marker is lines and a label, follows the person when dragged, is removed with the person, and hides when people are hidden. Five new checks in the regression suite (now 52) confirm the hand placement, the 1.75 m reading, that the marker follows and is removed with the person, and that it is neither exported nor an occluder.

v2.96 changes: PoE++ support for PrimeX 120 / 120W / 260. Per OptiTrack's documentation these need PoE++ (IEEE 802.3bt Type 4), drawing up to 90W with 100W allocated per switch port; they were previously planned at 30W, and the only edge switch was the GS728TPPv3, which is PoE+ (30W per port) and can't power them at all. Changes: those cameras now carry 90W draw / 100W allocation and a PoE++ flag (260W assumed to match the 260); switches gain a model — GS728TPPv3 (PoE+, 380W), GSM4230UP (PoE++, 90W per port, OptiTrack's PoE++ switch from the price list; 1440W budget assumed) or the M4300-28G Bridge — selectable on each edge switch's card and saved with the layout; switch budgets now count each camera's allocation rather than its draw; the Power Summary shows each switch's PoE class and warns when a PoE++ camera is routed to a PoE+ switch; Truss Auto Switch places PoE++ cameras on their own GSM4230UP switches (12 cameras or fewer, within budget at 100W each) and everything else on GS728TPPv3s; the quote lists GS728TPPv3 and GSM4230UP switches as separate lines. Verified with the regression suite, now 47 checks: on the Luma layout with a PrimeX 120 perimeter, all 16 PoE++ cameras land on 2 GSM4230UP switches (8 each, 800W of 1440W reserved), the 72 SlimX on six GS728TPPv3s, nothing is flagged, and forcing a PoE++ camera onto a PoE+ switch is flagged. VersaX 120 models are not confirmed and stay at 30W.

v2.95 changes: Ladder, triangle and single-tube truss. The truss builder only knew 4-point box sections; it now also draws 2-point ladder (two chords one above the other, rungs and zig-zag diagonals), 3-point triangle (equilateral, apex down, laced on all three faces) and single tube. Added Global Truss F22 and F32 (ladder, 220/290 mm), F23 and F33 (triangle, 220/290 mm) and F31 (50 mm single tube), with their series' piece lengths, in both the Truss type dropdown and the designer's GAUGE list. Legs and designer connectors stay square boxes, and a Milos gauge is always a box. Truss Auto Switch can snap switches onto the truss (new option, on by default): each switch moves to the nearest truss member that is actually drawn — the Manual Truss Designer's applied layout, or the Primary Ring truss plus any grid rails — sits on top of it, is spread out if two would land together, and the status line reports the furthest move; pins are recalculated after snapping, so the 12-camera and 380W limits still hold. Regression test suite delivered alongside the app (target3d_regression_tests.js, run with node target3d_regression_tests.js index.html, no installs): 41 checks covering script syntax, the EN/ES dictionaries, truss lengths and shapes, the camera grid, Truss Auto Switch, the save/load round trip and the cable report in both languages. Verified: all 41 pass on this build, and run against v2.92 the suite reports that build's misplaced Truss type translations; the new shapes draw 2/3/1 chords at the correct section sizes (F22 220 mm, F23 220 mm side, F31 50 mm); on the 88-camera Luma layout every snapped switch sits exactly on a member with 11 cameras each.

v2.94 changes: A batch of fixes and improvements from the review list. 10 Gb Bridge switch — the Bridge is now quoted as the NETGEAR M4300-28G (24 × 1 Gb + 4 × 10 Gb, SKU SWT1061) instead of a second GS728TPPv3, priced from its USD list price through the quote's normal currency conversion; Truss Auto Switch gives the Bridge 28 ports, names it in its summary, and warns if more than 24 edge switches would exceed its 1 Gb ports. Camera PoE figures set from the user's guidance: smaller Primes and all Slims 15W, bigger cameras (PrimeX 22 and up, VersaX, Prime 17W/41, Prime Colour) 30W — 21 models changed; not yet checked against optitrack.com datasheets. Save/load merged into one routine. Save Layout, presets and share links each built their own save object and each had its own loader, and each missed different things: Save Layout dropped the wall height (it only saved sliders up to s24), Load Layout never restored library assets or camera custom IDs/serials even though they were saved, presets never saved racks, switches, library assets or camera IDs and never refreshed the walls list, and share links skipped library assets. All three now use one snapshot builder and one restore. The Secondary Ring (counts, height, floor, stairs, camera model) and the designer's Milos gauge are now saved too, and loaded individual cameras no longer risk reusing an existing camera id. New "Clear camera pins" button with a live count, for when grid changes leave pins pointing at the wrong cameras. Standard truss lengths unified — the 3D view used a 1.5 m piece the Truss Component Report never listed; the report now uses the same list. More of the app translated — the grid preview line, Truss Auto Switch messages and confirmation, switch cards, Power Summary and the full Cable Report now follow the EN/ES setting and update when you switch language. Verified against the real code: a save → load → save round trip through the merged routines is identical for every object type (sliders s0–s29 including wall height, racks, library assets, switches and pins, people, TVs, walls with cutouts, camera IDs); a partial preset only changes what it contains; Secondary Ring settings and a Milos gauge survive save/load while a stale gauge can't override F14; the Cable Report, Power Summary and grid preview were checked in both languages.

v2.93 changes: Language bug fix — Truss type text was in the wrong language. When the Truss type dropdown was added (v2.89), its Spanish translations were inserted into the English dictionary instead of the Spanish one, right after the English entries. In an object literal the later duplicate key wins, so with the app in English the Truss type label, the Standard option and the hint showed in Spanish ("Tipo de estructura:", "Estructura de caja estándar"), while in Spanish they stayed English because the Spanish dictionary had no such keys. The six keys (label, Standard, F14, F24, F34, hint) are now in the right dictionaries, and the hint was rewritten in both languages to cover F14, F24 and F34 rather than F14 only. A full audit of the dictionaries against every data-i18n use in the page found nothing else: no other duplicate or missing keys, no garbled text, no entity problems. Verified by running the real language-apply logic in both directions (English → Spanish → English) against the real dictionaries.

v2.92 changes: Added Global Truss F24 (220 mm) and F34 (290 mm). Both are 4-point square box sections, the only shape the app draws. F24: 220 × 220 mm, 35 mm main tubes (chord centres 185 mm), pieces 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 4.0 m. F34: 290 × 290 mm, 50 mm main tubes (chord centres 240 mm), pieces 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 5.0 m. They appear in both the Truss type dropdown (Show truss) and the Truss Designer's GAUGE list, which now stay in step for every Global Truss type rather than just F14 (the sync that stops a Milos gauge override silently beating the type was generalised). The new piece lengths use the same fewest-custom-cuts-first splitter as F14, with new colours for 5 m, 3.5 m and 750 mm. Web (diagonal) tube sizes are assumed (16 mm F24, 20 mm F34) since only the main tubes were given. Not added: the ladder (F22, F32), triangle (F23, F33) and single-tube (F31) formats, because they need different cross-section geometry rather than another size — available as a follow-up. Verified against the real code: the drawn external size is exactly 100, 220 and 290 mm for F14, F24 and F34; for both new types, across 181 lengths every split sums exactly, uses only stocked lengths plus at most one trailing cut, and matches an independent brute-force search for fewest cuts then fewest pieces (F34 11 m = 5 + 5 + 1 m); and the two selectors agree through every sequence including Milos-then-F34 and layout loads. Still no truss pricing.

v2.91 changes: F14 is now in the Manual Truss Designer's GAUGE list, and the two truss selectors can no longer contradict each other. The designer already had its own GAUGE dropdown (Milos M222–M760); F14 had been added in a separate "Truss type" dropdown under Show truss instead, so it was missing from the place people look for truss sizes. Worse, the designer's gauges work by setting override values that win over the truss type, so after any Milos gauge had been picked, choosing F14 under Show truss silently did nothing. Now the GAUGE list has Default (original profile) and F14 — Global Truss (100mm) at the top (the old list showed M222 selected while the scene actually drew the default profile, so Default is now the honest starting state), and both controls drive the same setting: Default/F14 in the designer set the Truss type, a Milos gauge sets it back to Standard (it uses the standard piece lengths), and changing Truss type under Show truss updates the designer dropdown and clears any stale override. Loading a layout is authoritative — it resets the dropdown and any Milos override to what the file saved (older files: Standard). Verified against the real code through every sequence, including Milos then F14, F14 then back to Standard, and layout loads while a Milos gauge or F14 was active: the gauge actually drawn matched the selection every time (F14 0.04 m half-width, Default 0.18, M390 0.195). Not changed: Milos gauge choices still aren't saved in layouts, as before.

v2.90 changes: Global Truss F14 now uses its real stocked lengths. The Truss type selector added in v2.89 only changed the drawn profile; spans were still split into the standard truss's 250 mm–4 m pieces. Each truss type now carries its own length list: F14 uses Global Truss's nine straight lengths — 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5 and 3.0 m — for both the colour-coded 3D segments (new colours for 2.5 m, 400, 300 and 200 mm) and the Truss Component Report, whose "Standard lengths" line now lists the selected type's lengths. Splitting F14 spans largest-first would leave needless cuts with so many short lengths (0.6 m as 500 mm + a 100 mm cut), so F14 uses a search that minimises the custom-cut remainder first, then the piece count, preferring larger pieces; only one custom cut can ever remain and only when a span can't be made from stock (smallest F14 piece is 200 mm, so anything not a multiple of 100 mm needs one). The standard truss keeps its original largest-first behaviour untouched. Verified against the real code: for the standard truss the segments and report BOM are identical to the previous behaviour across 801 lengths from 0 to 40 m plus odd values; for F14, across 241 lengths every split sums exactly, uses only stocked lengths plus at most one trailing custom cut, and matches an independent brute-force search for fewest cuts then fewest pieces up to 6 m (e.g. 8 m = 3 + 3 + 2 m, 11 m = 3 + 3 + 3 + 2 m). Still not covered: pricing — there are no truss items in the product list.

v2.89 changes: New Truss type selector with the Global Truss F14. The app only ever had one fixed truss profile and no truss list, so this adds one: a "Truss type" dropdown under Show truss with Standard box truss (the original profile, still the default) and Global Truss F14 (compact 4-point decorative aluminium, 100 × 100 mm external, TÜV approved). The four gauge values every truss builder uses (chord spacing, depth, chord and web radius) were fixed constants; they are now driven by the selected type and re-applied at the start of every truss rebuild, so the ring truss, grid rails, legs and Truss Designer all follow the choice. Only the 100 mm external size was supplied, so F14's tube sizes are assumed (20 mm chords, 8 mm diagonals) — flagged in the code, Help and here. The grid rail "Half-size" setting would have drawn a non-existent 50 mm truss for F14, so for F14 it draws the real size. The Truss Component Report states the type in use. Saved in the layout; older layouts load as Standard. Not covered: F14's own stocked lengths (the report still uses the app's standard 250 mm–4 m pieces) and any pricing — there are no truss items in the product list to attach it to. Verified against the real code: the gauge switches both ways and rebuilds from the selector value, half-size grid rails scale correctly for each type, F14 comes out 100 mm external (80 mm chord centres + 20 mm tubes), save → load restores it and older files reset to Standard.

v2.88 changes: Camera Grid can now be set by total camera count. A new "Layout by" selector (Rows and columns / Total camera count) with a number box: type how many grid cameras you want and the grid works out the layout. It tries every row count from 1 to 40, spreads the cameras across the rows as evenly as it can (row counts never differ by more than one, with the extras spread out rather than bunched), and keeps the row count whose spacing along the room and across it is closest to equal — so typing 72 in a 16×8 room gives a 6×12 grid at about 1.4 m both ways rather than a stretched 4×18. Numbers that don't make a neat rectangle (e.g. 97) get a few tighter rows instead of a gap. In this mode the Rows/Columns sliders display the result (so grid truss rails and Dims stay in step) and are greyed out, and the preview line now reports the real spacing in metres in both modes. Capped at 1000 cameras; Rows and Columns slider maximums raised to 40 and 80. Saved in the layout (new fields in the extra block); older files load as rows × columns even if the app was last left in total mode. Verified against the real code across 15 totals including primes, 1, 2, 3, 600 and 1000 in several room shapes: every total produced exactly that many cameras, evenly spaced in X and Z to floating-point precision, inside the margins, with unique labels; blank/invalid input keeps the last good value; save → load → resize round trip re-spreads the same total across the new room. Known limit: with a staggered layout, column rails can't line up with every camera (row rails always do).

v2.87 changes: New "Truss Auto Switch" button (top of Network Switches) that works out and places the switches from the cameras in the scene. It uses the fewest switches that keep each to 12 cameras or fewer and inside the 380W PoE budget (power can force extra switches when cameras are heavy — e.g. 90W cameras fit only four per switch), groups cameras into evenly sized clusters with a capacity-limited k-means (deterministic, so the same design gives the same plan), and puts each switch at its cluster's centre at truss height (highest camera + 0.3m), lettered front-to-back and left-to-right. More than 24 cameras adds a Bridge switch next to the rack with Star to Bridge topology; 24 or fewer sets Daisy-chain to rack with no Bridge. Because nearest-switch routing ignores capacity, any camera it would pull onto the wrong switch is pinned with a per-camera override — only where needed. Supporting fix: grid cameras were labelled "Individual #id" with ids reallocated on every rebuild, so anything keyed by label (switch assignments, custom IDs/serials) silently reset whenever the grid regenerated; they are now labelled by position ("Grid 2-5"), which stays stable, also making the Cable Report readable. It replaces existing switches after a confirmation, and counts only visible cameras (it says so if individual/grid cameras are hidden). Tested against the real shipped code: the 88-camera Luma layout gets 8 switches + a Bridge at 11 cameras each (peak 210W), 24 cameras gives 2 switches with no Bridge and 25 gives 3 plus a Bridge, a 30-camera 90W case needs 8 switches, single-switch and one-camera cases work, daisy-chain uplinks come out A→rack and B→A, and pins survive a grid rebuild.

v2.86 changes: Camera Grid settings now save and reload properly, and a reloaded grid stays live. Save Layout (and saved presets and share links) only ever stored the numbered sliders and checkboxes, so the grid's own controls — rows, columns, height, margin, camera model, enable, rail mode and rail size — never reached the JSON, along with the switch display options, Cable Routes and the three 3D camera styles. Worse, the grid's generated cameras were being saved as ordinary individual cameras and the loader then switched the grid off, so a reloaded grid was a frozen copy that no longer followed room size or rows/columns — which is why editing the room afterwards did nothing. Now: grid-generated cameras are left out of the saved individual cameras (they are regenerated), all of the above is stored in a new extra block, and loading restores it after the individual cameras so the live grid switches itself back on and re-spreads at the current room size. Applies to Save/Load Layout, saved presets and share links; older files still load (a layout that only lists the grid enable checkbox gets the grid back on; files from before this fix keep their grid as static cameras). Verified with a save → load → resize round trip against the real grid code: manual cameras kept, grid cameras not double-saved, model/rails/styles/Cable Routes/switches restored, and after resizing to 24×10 with 5 rows × 20 columns the grid spans 0.5→23.5 and 0.5→9.5 with even spacing. The Luma Arles layout is rewritten in the new format.

v2.85 changes: Dims: added the margin dimension — when Grid margin pulls the grid truss rails in from the room's walls, a new horizontal measurement now shows exactly how far the first/last rail sits in from the wall (one for rows, one for columns, each only drawn when that axis's margin is actually non-zero), independent of the rail-to-rail spacing and the vertical rail-to-ceiling/rail-to-perimeter-truss dimensions already in place — an installer gets the inset figure as well as the spacing and the drop heights. Verified with isolated tests: correct distance for a real margin value, no dimension at all when margin is zero, and correct clamping when margin exceeds half the room's width. Luma Arles layout rebuilt to the user's original spec of 9 edge GS728TPPv3 switches + 1 Bridge (10 nodes total, matching "9 switches plus a bridging switch" exactly, rather than the earlier 8+1 approximation). Reaching a 9th switch from the grid's natural 4-rows-by-2-halves split meant one row has to take 3 segments instead of 2 (9 isn't evenly divisible by 4) — tried seven different switch-count and placement combinations through the real shipped camera-placement and nearest-switch code before settling on this one, including an all-perimeter-combined variant and several row/wall-split mixes, picking whichever produced the tightest spread. The shipped layout needs no dedicated perimeter (N/S/E/W) switches at all: with all 4 grid rows getting their own switches, the outer rows already sit close enough to the perimeter walls to absorb those cameras naturally, which previous attempts confirmed empirically. Final distribution is 8–12 cameras per switch (88 total, average 9.78), 105–150W per switch — comfortably inside the 380W budget throughout — verified against the real shipped placement, nearest-switch resolution, and star uplink topology code, with all 88 cameras assigned and all 10 uplink links (9 edge→Bridge, 1 Bridge→rack) correctly present. Full syntax check and entity sweep clean throughout.

v2.84 changes: Two more items from user testing. Switches are now draggable in the 3D view — click and drag a switch's body the same way a rack, TV or person already drags, on a horizontal plane at its current height (its Y stays set via the sidebar's Y field, matching how it was already described as "fully draggable afterward via the X/Y/Z fields"). This needed its own click-handling added from scratch: switches had `clickable` set on their outer group only, which raycasting never actually hits (it hits the mesh underneath), so nothing happened when you clicked one before now — the body and LED meshes now carry the clickable flag and a reference back to the switch, and dragging writes the new position straight back into the underlying switches[] entry (not just the visible 3D group), so the move survives the next full rebuild instead of silently snapping back. Cables now update live while dragging a switch — exactly the same "move it, watch the cable follow" behaviour the equipment rack already had, extended to switches: every camera routed to that switch, and its own backbone link, redraws on every mouse-move frame rather than only after you let go. Dims: added the rail-to-perimeter-truss gap — when the Primary Ring's own truss is also shown (Show truss), a second vertical dimension now appears (at the opposite corner from the rail-to-ceiling one, so the two don't overlap) giving the gap between the grid rails and that perimeter truss specifically, since the two structures can sit at different heights and installers need both figures, not just the one to the ceiling. Verified with isolated tests: the position write-back survives a simulated rebuild without snapping back, and the perimeter-truss gap math correctly produces a real figure, skips cleanly when the perimeter truss is hidden, and skips cleanly when the two structures happen to sit at the same height (nothing to dimension). Full syntax check and entity sweep clean throughout.

v2.83 changes: Five items from user testing of the Network Switches and Cable Routes features. Cable Report bug fixed — the report was still written against the pre-switches data model: it assumed every entry in the shared cables list was a camera cable, so the moment any Network Switch was placed, reading a switch backbone cable's non-existent cameraId crashed the report outright. Camera and backbone cables are now handled separately: camera cable rows show which switch (or the rack) each camera actually connects to, a new Switch Assignments section lists every switch's cameras grouped together, and a new Backbone/Uplink section lists the switch-to-switch and switch-to-rack runs with their own lengths and a subtotal — verified against the real shipped report code with both a mixed camera+backbone scenario (the exact case that used to crash) and the legacy no-switches case, confirming it still reads "→ Rack" exactly as before when no switches are placed. Switches now named with letters (A, B, C… continuing past Z as AA, AB…) instead of the old "S1"/"Bridge1" numbering, so a switch's identifier never looks like a camera's — tested at the Z→AA rollover. Switch labels made more obvious — the floating 3D tag is now a solid colour-coded card (teal for Bridge, dark blue-grey for edge) with a bright border and large white text, rather than small ghost-coloured text with no background, so it reads clearly from a distance instead of blending into the scene. "Truss Routing (right-angle)" renamed to "Cable Routes" in the Assets menu, Help docs, and both language files — shorter and reads better as a toggle label. New "Dims" overlay (next to Grid truss rails) draws the installation measurements an installer actually needs: the spacing between adjacent grid truss rails, and the vertical gap from the rails up to the room's ceiling height for drop-hanger or clamp-extension sizing — drawn as dimension lines with tick marks and distance labels straight into the 3D scene (requires Grid truss rails set to something other than Off), so they show up automatically in any screenshot once switched on; the spacing and gap maths were verified against hand-calculated expected values for a 4-row/18-column grid. The shipped Luma Arles layout has also been updated: its switches are renamed A–H (edge) and I (Bridge) to match. Full syntax check and entity sweep clean throughout — the sweep itself caught one genuine `&`-in-textContent bug in the new Dims checkbox label, fixed before shipping.

v2.82 changes: Four fixes/additions from user feedback on the Network Switches feature. Quote generation bug fixed — Generate Quote from Design was still using an old total-camera-count heuristic for its network switch line item, hardcoded to qty 1 regardless of how many switches were actually placed in the design; it now counts the real edge and Bridge switches when any exist, using the NETGEAR ProSafe GS728TPPv3 (added to the product database, 380W PoE budget, £954.08 — alongside the existing GS728TPPv2 entry, not replacing it), falling back to the old tiered heuristic only when no switches have been placed at all. "Master" renamed to "Bridge Switch" throughout the UI, Help docs, and both language files, per user feedback that "Master" read as master/slave terminology — the underlying data field is untouched (still `role:'master'` internally) so existing saved layouts keep working without any migration. New right-angle cable routing option (Assets → Truss Routing) — every cable (camera-to-switch, camera-to-rack, and switch backbones) can now be drawn as a route that only travels vertically or horizontally at truss height, in right angles, rather than a direct diagonal line, addressing feedback that the default view — while visually clean — doesn't reflect how a cable is actually run along truss bars; off by default, toggle either way per preference. Verified with isolated tests against the real shipped code: the quote logic across four scenarios (no switches, a full 12-edge design, a small design, and a Bridge-only edge case), and the orthogonal router's point sequence and axis-alignment across four geometric cases including the same-position edge case. Full syntax check and entity sweep clean throughout.

v2.81 changes: Network Switches Phase 3 & 4 — uplink topology and power budgeting. Uplink topology: a new Star to Master / Daisy-chain to rack selector. Star sends every edge switch's backbone cable directly to the Master switch (or straight to the rack with no Master placed). Daisy-chain has each switch hop to whichever neighbouring switch is both nearest and itself closer to the rack, walking toward the rack switch-by-switch — a switch already closest among all switches uplinks directly rather than searching for a neighbour. The Master's own link to the rack is always drawn, independent of mode. These backbone cables render as genuinely thicker tube meshes (not `THREE.Line`, whose width WebGL frequently ignores), colour-matched to their origin switch, alongside the existing thin per-camera cables. Power budgeting: every camera model now carries a placeholder PoE draw figure (15–90W, flagged clearly as an estimate pending real datasheet figures — not taken from actual OptiTrack specs). Each switch's card shows a live PoE load vs its budget, turning red with a warning if oversubscribed. A new Power Summary panel lists every switch's load plus a count of AC power drops needed (one per switch — separate from PoE, since a switch needs its own mains feed regardless of how many cameras it powers over PoE). Verified with isolated tests against the actual shipped code: star mode, chain mode's hop-by-hop pattern, the no-master-direct-to-rack fallback, PoE load aggregation across multiple switches and camera models, over-budget flagging, the AC-drop count, and the backbone builder's zero-length edge case; full syntax check and entity sweep clean throughout.

v2.80 changes: Network Switches Phase 2 — camera-to-switch cable assignment and colour-coding. Every camera now auto-routes its cable to its nearest edge switch (master switches are correctly excluded as a camera target, since they aggregate switches rather than serve cameras directly) whenever at least one edge switch is placed; with none placed, cables route straight to the rack exactly as before this feature existed. Cables are colour-coded per switch — a deterministic colour per switch id, so the same switch keeps the same colour across rebuilds without needing to store one — making it easy to see at a glance which cameras share a switch. Added a manual override: click any camera to open the existing Camera Alignment panel, now with an Assigned Switch dropdown (found the panel was already the one place that works for any camera regardless of system — wall/ring cameras have no persistent object of their own, only a stable label, which is exactly what that panel's existing Custom ID/Serial mechanism already keys off). A stale override (its switch got deleted) falls back to nearest-switch cleanly rather than losing the cable. Both the switch list and the override map now round-trip through Save/Load Layout. This phase still only routes cameras to their switch — the switch-to-switch/master uplink and the switch-to-rack backbone aren't modelled yet (Phase 3), so a cable currently ends at the switch. Verified with isolated tests against the actual shipped routing code: legacy no-switches fallback, nearest-switch resolution and colouring, override precedence and its stale-override fallback, and two save/load round-trips; full syntax check clean throughout.

v2.79 changes: New Network Switches section (Phase 1 of a larger networking/cabling feature) — models switches placed up in the truss to keep camera-to-switch Cat6A runs short, matching how larger warehouse-scale installs are actually cabled. Add Switch / Add Master Switch buttons place a switch at the Primary Ring's truss height by default, fully repositionable via X/Y/Z fields on each switch's card; each switch has an editable name, role (Edge/Master), port count, and PoE budget (W). Rendered in 3D as a small box (master switches in teal, edge switches in grey) with a floating name label. Fully wired into Save/Load Layout, including correct id continuation after a reload. This phase covers placement only — camera-to-switch cable assignment (auto nearest-switch with manual override), switch-to-switch/master uplink topology (star and daisy-chain), and PoE/power-budget reporting are planned as follow-on phases. Verified via isolated logic tests (add/remove/naming/default-position, and a full save→load round-trip including the empty-array case); full syntax check clean.

v2.78 changes: Small robustness fix while rebuilding a client layout: Load Layout now correctly restores the Camera Grid's on-screen slider labels (Rows/Columns/Height/Margin) — previously only sN-style sliders had their number label synced on load; the grid's own range sliders use a different id convention and were silently skipped, so the underlying camera generation was always correct but the displayed numbers next to those sliders could lag until manually touched. No visible UI change otherwise.

v2.77 changes: Grid truss rails now sit above the grid's camera height (+0.3m) instead of at the same height as the cameras — matching the Primary Ring's own established convention (its truss has always sat 0.3m above its cameras; the grid rails just weren't following that pattern yet). Also found and fixed a mislabelling from v2.72: the value read for the grid rails' third parameter was "Truss brightness" (opacity), not a size control as the variable name implied — real beam size comes from separate gauge constants the grid rails weren't touching at all. Added a genuine Rail size control (Full truss / Half-size truss / Simple rail), defaulting to Half-size since a dense grid with many rails can look cluttered at full truss scale; Simple rail skips the lattice geometry entirely for a single thin beam. Verified the height offset at multiple camera heights, the half-size gauge values, that full-size correctly falls through to the normal defaults, that gauge overrides are cleanly restored afterward with no leakage between calls, and that Simple rail mode never calls the lattice builder at all.

v2.76 changes: Larger Style up 15% — 1.1475x → 1.319625x, per feedback.

v2.75 changes: Larger Style halved — 2.295x → 1.1475x, per feedback. Still modestly bigger than PrimeX Style's own cube (0.1377m vs 0.12m per side) so it remains distinguishable as "the larger one", just far more subtly now.

v2.74 changes: Larger Style reduced a further 15% — 2.7x → 2.295x — per feedback that it was still reading too big.

v2.73 changes: Fixed both new camera 3D styles from v2.72, against real SlimX reference photos. Slim Style was slim in the wrong axis — it was built long in depth (toward the lens) and thin in height/width, like a pencil; real SlimX cameras are the opposite: thin in depth, roughly square face. Rebuilt with depth as the smallest dimension (0.04) and a square face (0.115 × 0.115, close to PrimeX's 0.12 cube so the two read as similarly-sized but differently-shaped), plus a chrome-style lens bezel matching the reference photos. Larger Style reduced from 3x to 2.7x scale (~10% smaller), matching feedback that it was reading too big. Updated the Help text (English and Spanish) that described the old geometry to match.
